summary: Defines an experimental ICMP message type for IPv4 used with the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP). It dynamically updates identifier and locator bindings for an existing ILNP session. It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group.

eli5.summary: When a computer moves to a new place on the network, this message tells its friend the new address so the chat keeps going. It is only an experiment.

questions: how does ilnp update locators on ipv4
what is the ilnpv4 locator update message
how does ilnp handle node mobility
when should a node send a locator update advertisement
subtitle: An ICMP message that tells ILNP nodes when addresses change on the network.

tldr.problem: In ILNP for IPv4, a node might acquire new network addresses (Locators) as it moves or multihomes. Its communicating peers need to learn about these changes to keep sending packets to the right place.
tldr.mechanism: A new ICMP message type (253) carries a list of the sender's currently valid Locators, with preference rankings and validity periods. Recipients can acknowledge receipt or update their routing information.
tldr.outcome: This is an experimental proposal that remains undeployed, as ILNP itself is only experimental and has not been adopted by the Internet community.

today: RFC 6745 is an Experimental protocol from the IRTF Routing Research Group published in November 2012. It remains experimental and has not been adopted for deployment.

sections.title: Introduction to ILNP and Locator Changes
sections.content:
This RFC is part of the ILNP document set, a set of experimental proposals for evolving the Internet. ILNP separates the concept of a network address into two pieces: a Locator (which is topology-dependent and used for routing) and an Identifier (which is topology-independent and identifies the node itself).

When an ILNP node's set of valid Locators changes—because it has moved, acquired a new network connection, or lost an old one—it needs a way to tell its communication partners about the change. This document defines an ICMP message that does exactly that.
sections.eli5: Think of a Locator like your street address and an Identifier like your name. When you move to a new house, you need to tell your friends your new address.

sections.title: The ICMP Locator Update Message Format
sections.content:
The message uses ICMP Type 253 (reserved for experimental use in RFC 4727) with Code 0. The message contains:

  • Type: Always 253.
  • Code: Always 0.
  • Num of Locs: How many Locator values follow.
  • Operation: Either 0x01 for an Advertisement ("here are my new addresses") or 0x02 for an Acknowledgement ("I received your advertisement").
  • Locator [i]: Each is a 32-bit value representing a valid network address.
  • Preference [i]: A relative ranking of each Locator's desirability, matching the preference semantics in ILNP DNS records.
  • Lifetime [i]: How many seconds each Locator should be considered valid.

A sender announcing a Locator change MUST include all currently valid Locators in a single message. Recipients receiving a valid advertisement MUST send an Acknowledgement back and update their cache with the new Locator set.
sections.eli5: The message is like a list saying "I can now be reached at addresses 10.1.1.5 and 10.2.2.3, and I prefer the first one for the next hour."

sections.title: Security and Authentication Requirements
sections.content:
This message MUST ONLY be used in the context of an active ILNP session. Authentication is always required. Every ICMP Locator Update message MUST include an ILNPv4 Identifier Option (from RFC 6746) and an ILNPv4 Nonce Option.

The Nonce is a cryptographically random 64-bit value that is unique to each direction of communication. A receiver checks the nonce value before accepting the message, defeating off-path attackers who do not know the correct nonce. If the nonce is wrong or missing, the packet is discarded as a forgery.

Deployments in high-threat environments SHOULD also protect these messages using IPsec (RFC 4301). Even when IPsec is used, the Nonce Option must still be present.
sections.eli5: Before you believe the message, you check a secret number that only real friends know. That prevents someone on the internet from lying about being you.

sections.title: How Nodes Use the Message
sections.content:
A node detects that its Locator set has changed and composes a Locator Update Advertisement. It sends this to each ILNP correspondent node (each node it is actively communicating with) as a unicast ICMP message.

Each correspondent node receives the message, verifies the Identifier Option, checks the Nonce, and if everything is valid, updates its local cache of that node's valid Locators. The receiving node then sends a Locator Update Acknowledgement back to the sender, echoing the same message body but with Operation set to 0x02.

Multihomed nodes or sites with many upstream connections might need to advertise a large number of Locators in a single message. Implementations must be prepared to handle such messages without overflow or performance degradation.
sections.eli5: Node A says "I have these addresses now." Node B says "OK, I got it" and remembers them. If A loses a connection, it sends a new list without that address.

sections.title: Backwards Compatibility and Transport Independence
sections.content:
The Locator Update message has no direct impact on transport protocols like TCP or UDP. ILNP is designed to decouple transport-layer sessions (which bind to Identifiers) from network-layer changes (which affect Locators only).

When ILNPv4 is not in use, an IPv4 node MUST discard these ICMP Type 253 messages without processing them. The checksum is calculated using the standard IPv4 ICMP checksum algorithm.

Note that ICMP Type 253 is shared experimental space; other experiments may also use this type value for different purposes. Implementations should code defensively.
sections.eli5: A regular IPv4 computer ignores this message because it does not understand ILNP. TCP and UDP programs do not notice the address change because ILNP keeps them talking to the same Identifier.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment Considerations
sections.content:
To support ILNPv4, nodes need a mode bit in their network layer to track which sessions are classic IPv4 and which are ILNPv4 mode. Nodes also need an Identifier Locator Communication Cache (ILCC) as described in RFC 6741 to map Identifiers to sets of Locators.

When a Locator Update Advertisement arrives, the receiver replaces its entire cached Locator set for that sender with the new set received in the message. The implementation must handle multiple Locators per node efficiently and support policy-based Locator selection.

This is an experimental protocol from the IRTF Routing Research Group. Implementations are for research and evaluation only.
sections.eli5: A computer running ILNP keeps a special list of which Identifiers go with which addresses, and updates it when messages arrive.
